Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Title

Data about us: privacy, consent and the law

Personal data belongs to the person it describes. Collect only what you need, ask first, keep it safe — it is the law in Nigeria.

Next Generation Genius · Year 1 · Foundation

Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Goals

By the end of today

  • Say what personal data is
  • Explain consent and collecting only what you need
  • Name Nigeria's data protection law and what it promises
Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Idea 1

Understand it

Personal data is anything that identifies a person: name, phone number, photo, address, location, and combinations ("the only 13-year-old drummer at Egbeda").

Three rules for anybody collecting it:

  1. Consent — ask, and say what it is for. For a child, a parent consents.
  2. Minimise — collect only what you need. A survey about lunch does not need phone numbers.
  3. Protect — keep it safe, share it with nobody, delete it when you are done.
Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Idea 2

Understand it

In Nigeria the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA) sets these rules, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission enforces them. You have rights too: to know what is held about you, and to ask for it to be corrected or deleted.

Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Key words

Key words

Personal data
information that identifies a living person
Consent
permission given knowingly and freely
Data minimisation
collecting only what you need
Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Practice

Now you do it

  1. Sort a list into personal and not personal data
  2. Find three apps' privacy settings and turn one off
  3. Rewrite a survey to collect less

Need a hand? For each item ask: could this help someone find or recognise me?

Done early? Design an anonymous version of your survey and explain how you would still spot duplicate answers.

Data Appreciation · Week 9 · Assessment

How you will be assessed

  • Your survey asks about favourite lunches. Which field should you REMOVE?
  • Give two things a person collecting your data should do to follow the law.
  • Which piece of data about you would you least want shared, and why? (Answer is private to your instructor.)

Your work is marked against the rubric, and you may be asked to explain your choices. Show your own thinking.
